6: ## Files:
7:     - simulation_HN_NOE.dat:
8:         contains the backcalculated HN-NOEs for each 1 ns frame in the simulation. Rows = timestep/frame (ns),  columns = atompair in HN-NOE. First column is timestep/frame. Columns are orderede as in experimental file.  
9:     - simulation_methyl_NOE.dat
10:         same as above but for methyl NOE pairs
11:     - simulation_SAXS.dat: 
12:         contains the backcalculated scatter (SAXS) intensity for each 1 ns frame in the simulation. Rows = timestep/frame (ns), columns = q_i 
13:     - BME_simulation_weights.dat
14:         contains the optimized weights for each simulation frame from the BME method. 
15:     - BME_stats_SAXS.dat
16:         SAXS from simulation  after BME reweight
17:     - BME_stats_methyl_NOE.dat
18:          Methyl NOE from simulation  after BME reweight
19:      - hyperparameter_theta.dat
20:         contains calculated chi^2 vs Srel for determination of the hyperparameter theta in the BME method. 
21:     - exp_HN2_NOE.dat
22:         HN NOE experimental file from (2), excluding any intraresidues. 
23:     - exp_methyl_NOE.dat
24:         NOE experimental file from (2), excluding any intraresidues.
25:     - the experimental SAXS file used for reweighting can be found in SAXS_and_SANS directory.

23:                                     Abstract Nanodiscs are membrane mimetics that consist of a protein belt surrounding a lipid
24:                                     bilayer, and are broadly used for characterization of membrane proteins. Here, we investigate the
25:                                     structure, dynamics and biophysical properties of two small nanodiscs, MSP1D1DH5 and DH4H5.
26:                                     We combine our SAXS and SANS experiments with molecular dynamics simulations and previously
27:                                     obtained NMR and EPR data to derive and validate a conformational ensemble that represents the
28:                                     structure and dynamics of the nanodisc. We find that it displays conformational heterogeneity with
29:                                     various elliptical shapes, and with substantial differences in lipid ordering in the centre and rim of
30:                                     the discs. Together, our results reconcile previous apparently conflicting observations about the
31:                                     shape of nanodiscs, and pave the way for future integrative studies of larger complex systems such
32: *For correspondence:                as membrane proteins embedded in nanodiscs.

67:                                    experiments have been complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations that provided both
68:                                    pioneering insights into the structure (Shih et al., 2005; Shih et al., 2007) as well as a better under-
69:                                    standing of the assembly process, lipid-protein interactions and how much a nanodisc mimicks
70:                                    the membrane bilayer (Siuda and Tieleman, 2015; Debnath and Schäfer, 2015;
71:                                    Vestergaard et al., 2015).
72:                                        A high resolution structure of the MSP protein belt encircling the nanodisc was recently obtained
73:                                    from the small, helix-5-deleted nanodisc, MSP1D1DH5 (henceforth DH5), reconstituted with DMPC
74:                                    lipids (DH5-DMPC) (Bibow et al., 2017) by combining nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectros-
75:                                    copy, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and transmission electron microscopy
76:                                    (TEM) (Bibow et al., 2017). While these experiments were performed on lipid-loaded nanodiscs, the
77:                                    study focused on the protein components, and on determining a time- and ensemble averaged
78:                                    structure of these, but left open the question of the role of the lipids (Martinez et al., 2017) as well
79:                                    as any structural dynamics of the overall nanodisc. Intriguingly, the resulting structure of the belt pro-
80:                                    teins corresponded to that of an almost circularly-shaped disc, while our previous SAXS/SANS inves-
81:                                    tigations are clearly consistent with discs with an on-average elliptical cross-section (Skar-
82:                                    Gislinge et al., 2010; Midtgaard et al., 2015).
83:                                        Here, we build upon this work to study the structure and dynamics of the nanodisc and the lipid
84:                                    properties in the disc. We performed SAXS and SANS experiments on the DH5-DMPC variant, and
85:                                    integrated these with MD simulations and the NMR data (Bibow et al., 2017) through an integrative
86:                                    Bayesian/maximum entropy (BME) approach (Hummer and Köfinger, 2015; Różycki et al., 2011;
87:                                    Bottaro et al., 2020; Bottaro et al., 2018; Orioli et al., 2020). We thereby obtain a model of the
88:                                    conformational ensemble of the DH5-DMPC nanodisc that is consistent with the structural informa-
89:                                    tion obtained from each method, as well as our molecular simulations, and which successfully
90:                                    explains differences in previous structural interpretations. In addition, we study the lipid ordering in
91:                                    our ensemble, and use the results to aid in the interpretation of Differential Scanning Calorimetry
92:                                    (DSC) measurements of the melting transition of DMPC in differently sized nanodiscs. Our study
93:                                    exemplifies how these integrative methods can be used to protein-lipid systems, possibly paving the
94:                                    way for future studies of membrane proteins embedded in nanodiscs.

98:                                    Results and discussion
99:                                    Structural investigations of DH5-DMPC and DH4H5-DMPC nanodiscs by
100:                                    SAXS and SANS
101:                                    We determined optimal reconstitution ratios between the DMPC lipids and the DH5 and DH4H5 pro-
102:                                    tein belts to form lipid-saturated nanodiscs based on a size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) analysis
103:                                    (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods). In line with previous studies
104:                                    (Hagn et al., 2013), we found that reconstitution ratios of 1:33 for DH4H5:DMPC and 1:50 for DH5:
105:                                    DMPC were optimal in order to form single and relatively narrow symmetric peaks. Building upon
106:                                    earlier work for other discs (Denisov et al., 2004; Skar-Gislinge et al., 2010) we performed com-
107:                                    bined SEC-SAXS and SEC-SANS experiments to determine the size and shape of DMPC loaded DH5
108:                                    and DH4H5 nanodiscs (Figure 1). These experiments were performed at 10˚C, and based on results
109:                                    from previous NMR experiments on nanodiscs (Martinez et al., 2017) as well as a melting tempera-
110:                                    ture TM » 24˚C for DMPC, where we expect the lipids to be in the gel-phase. Our SAXS and SANS
111:                                    data all exhibit a flat Guinier region at low q and indicate no signs of aggregation (Figure 1A,B). In
112:                                    both the DH5-DMPC and DH4H5-DMPC systems, the SAXS data exhibit an oscillation at medium to
113:                                    high q ([0.05:0.2] Å-1) arising from the combination of a negative excess scattering length density of
114:                                    the hydrophobic alkyl-chain bilayer core and positive excess scattering length densities of the hydro-
115:                                    philic lipid PC-headgroups and the amphipathic protein belt. The SANS data decreases monotoni-
116:                                    cally as a function of q in accordance with the homogeneous contrast situation present here. These
117:                                    two different contrast situations, core-shell-contrast for SAXS and bulk-contrast for SANS, are also
118:                                    clearly reflected in the obtained p(r)-functions (Figure 1C,D), which also confirm that the DH5-DMPC
119:                                    nanodiscs are slightly larger than the DH4H5-DMPC nanodiscs.
120:                                       Our data are in qualitative agreement with the SAXS and SANS data obtained for MSP1D1 nano-
121:                                    discs (Denisov et al., 2004; Skar-Gislinge et al., 2010) and similar systems (Midtgaard et al., 2014;
122:                                    Midtgaard et al., 2015), and indicate an ‘on average’ discoidal structure. Therefore, w first analyzed

164:                                    2002), but in agreement with the very broad melting transition observed in our DSC data (see
165:                                    below). We find 65 ± 13 and 100 ± 14 DMPC molecules in the nanodiscs for DH4H5 and DH5, respec-

357:                                    Integrating experiments and simulations
358:                                    While the MD simulations are overall in good agreement with the SAXS and NMR NOE data, there
359:                                    remain discrepancies that could contain information about the conformational ensemble of DH5-
360:                                    DMPC in solution. We therefore used a previously described Bayesian/Maximum Entropy (BME)
361:                                    approach (Hummer and Köfinger, 2015; Różycki et al., 2011; Bottaro et al., 2018; Cesari et al.,
362:                                    2016; Bottaro et al., 2020) to integrate the MD simulations with the SAXS and NMR data. Briefly,
363:                                    the BME method refines the simulation against measured experimental averages by balancing (1)
364:                                    minimizing the discrepancy between the simulation and the observed experimental averages and (2)
365:                                    ensuring as little perturbation of the original simulation as possible thereby limiting chances of over-
366:                                    fitting. The outcome is a conformational ensemble that is more likely to represent DH5-DMPC in
367:                                    solution. In practice, this is achieved by changing the weight of each configuration in the ensemble
368:                                    obtained from the MD simulations, and we therefore call this a ‘reweighted ensemble’ (Bottaro and
369:                                    Lindorff-Larsen, 2018; Bottaro et al., 2020). The amount of reweighting can be quantified by an
370:                                    entropy change (Srel ) that reports on how much the weights had to be changed to fit the data
371:                                    (Bottaro et al., 2018) (see Materials and methods). Alternatively, the value feff ¼ expðSrel Þ reports
372:                                    on the effective ensemble size, that is what fraction of the original frames that were used to derive
373:                                    the final ensemble (Orioli et al., 2020). We note that we reweight each individual conformation in
374:                                    the ensemble, and thus that the clustering is only used for presenting the results. In this way we
375:                                    avoid uncertainties that come from difficulties in clustering heterogeneous ensembles.
376:                                        We used both the SAXS and NOE data individually, as well as combined, to understand the
377:                                    effects of each source of data on the reweighted conformational ensemble (Table 2). We note that
378:                                    when a specific type of data is used to generate the ensemble, the resulting c2 simply reports on
379:                                    how well the simulation has been fitted to the data; because of the maximum-entropy regularization
380:                                    to avoid overfitting, we do not fit the data as accurately as possible. The two types of experimental
381:                                    data complement each other in structural information content. Specifically, the SAXS data report on
382:                                    the overall size and shape, and is sensitive to both protein and lipids through atom-atom pair distri-
383:                                    butions in a range starting from » 10 Å, whereas the NOEs contain local, specific atom-atom distan-
384:                                    ces from the protein belts of the DH5 but not any direct information about the lipids.
385:                                        We find that refining against a single of the two data types only improves the MD trajectory with
386:                                    respect to the structural properties it is sensitive to, highlighting the orthogonal information in the
387:                                    two sources of information. In addition, we performed reweighting with the methyl NOEs and the
388:                                    amide NOEs separately (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The already low discrepancy of the amide
389:                                    NOEs barely improves while the discrepancies of both methyl NOEs and SAXS are unaffected by
390:                                    integration with amide NOEs alone, implying that the structural information content contained in the
391:                                    amide NOEs (mostly secondary structure) is already correctly captured by the force field and starting
392:                                    structure. Because the NOE and SAXS experiments provide independent information we refined the
393:                                    ensemble against both sets of data (Figure 3). We find that we can fit both sources of data at rea-
394:                                    sonable accuracy without dramatic changes of the weights away from the Boltzmann distribution of
395:                                    the force field (feff ¼ 18%).
